parts.label: Part 2
parts.title: Walking and shoes in eighteenth-century London
parts.subtitle: A look at changing fashions in footwear and leisure
parts.article:
Walking and shoes V2

A It was difficult to get about in eighteenth-century London. During the first half of that century, the physical mobility of the upper classes in the city had been considerably restricted: the poor condition of the streets did not allow ‘walking for pleasure’ outside private parks or pleasure gardens. Streets were dirty, rubbish was everywhere and the British climate did not help. Walking could be a risky business. The terrible state of roads, always flooded and muddy, created a metropolitan world of shoe cleaners and street sweepers.

B References to walking are not abundant in early eighteenth-century texts. This is truer for urban spaces than for places in the countryside, where country life had always been dominated by a lifestyle of outdoor activities. For instance, in eighteenth-century London, a sightseer’s experience was restricted to touristic places and involved journeys by a series of boats and coaches. Walking was considered to be an activity for the poorer members of society — or simply those who could not afford a coach.

C This situation underwent a sudden improvement in the mid-eighteenth century, with measures implementing the provision of public spaces in which to walk. The first legislation concerning paving in London was passed in 1762, and during the following decades similar laws were enacted in many cities. By the end of the century, areas for walking were commonplace, and far more people were enjoying the pastime than before. Sophie von La Roche writes about metropolitan street life in the diary of her visit to London of 1786. She comments on how many more pedestrians there were on the broad, clean pavements, alongside the houses where, she says ‘many thousands of neatly clad people, eminent men and dressy women, pursue their way safe from the carriages, horses and dirt’. Although the pastime of walking was pursued only in specific spaces designed for the purpose, the number of these spaces increased as the nineteenth century approached. Travelling on foot became smoother and less dangerous.

D Attitudes toward walking through public spaces and their changes over time were visible in the practical designs of fashionable footwear. Protective overshoes and other devices designed to keep feet above the dirty and wet ground soon disappeared, and ease of mobility increased. In the early eighteenth century, the look of men’s and women’s shoes started to diverge in appearance as a distinction between male and female footwear filtered into production. Contemporary descriptions of the boot and shoe trade underlined the differences between ladies’ shoemakers and men’s shoemakers too.

E The production of men’s and women’s footwear required different skills, as the products were essentially different. Men wore more sober footwear, not unlike modern shoes. Their shoes were entirely made of leather, which provided resistance to rain, mud and bad weather. Women’s shoes had uppers made of textiles — silk, satin or cloth — and their resistance to bad weather and dirty streets was limited. Only the lower ranks of women wore leather shoes of a form similar to men’s. The high-quality shoes for women were often embroidered and were normally worn with protective overshoes, as they were prone to being damaged or disfigured by the conditions of the time.

F The shoes of men and women related to their more general clothing in different ways. Wealthy women’s footwear harmonised with their other garments, a harmony that could be effected through matching textiles, general colour, embroidered detail or buckles. In the eighteenth century, men’s shoes matched their clothing in different ways, for example with glossy black, red or pink heels. The shoe of an upper-class man also acted as a type of sign which emphasised the difference between the wearer and young boys and women. The shoe also distinguished him from working men who wore leather or cloth protective leggings, ragged shoes and clogs. The symbolic marking of the entry of a wealthy young man into manhood through his shoes, as well as his other dress, may have been of more importance than has previously been acknowledged in costume history.

questions.question: details of a legal change affecting conditions in urban areas

analyses.content: C段明确提到了针对城市公共空间的“首个立法（first legislation）”和随后实施的“类似法律（similar laws）”，完美对应题目中的“法律变动（legal change）”细节。
你可能会在原文中死磕寻找“law”这个词，但要注意原文前半部分使用了“legislation（立法）”进行同义替换。

This situation underwent a sudden improvement in the mid-eighteenth century, with measures implementing the provision of public spaces in which to walk. The first legislation concerning paving in London was passed in 1762, and during the following decades similar laws were enacted in many cities.

questions.question: a reference to how the significance of men’s shoes has been overlooked by experts

analyses.content: F段最后一句提到，男鞋在象征意义上的重要性“比服装史中以往所承认的（previously been acknowledged）更重要”，这就对应了题目中一直被专家们“忽略（overlooked）”的含义。
不要被前面关于男鞋颜色的描述迷惑，只有看到“acknowledgement”在历史认同上的变化，才能对应出“被忽视”的核心考点。

The symbolic marking of the entry of a wealthy young man into manhood through his shoes, as well as his other dress, may have been of more importance than has previously been acknowledged in costume history.

questions.question: a reference to how gender began to affect shoe design

analyses.content: D段明确提到男鞋和女鞋的外观开始“分化（diverge）”，并且这种男女鞋的区分也渗透到了生产和鞋匠分类中，对应了性别开始影响鞋子设计。
你可能想选E段，因为E段讲了男女鞋的材质不同，但D段中的“started to diverge”才是讲述这种男女设计差异“开始（began to）”的源头。

In the early eighteenth century, the look of men’s and women’s shoes started to diverge in appearance as a distinction between male and female footwear filtered into production. Contemporary descriptions of the boot and shoe trade underlined the differences between ladies’ shoemakers and men’s shoemakers too.

questions.question: a description of potential problems faced in urban areas

analyses.content: A段详细描写了城市街道的恶劣状况，如“肮脏（dirty）”、“满是垃圾（rubbish）”、“经常被淹和泥泞（flooded and muddy）”，这些直接对应了城市地区面临的潜在“问题（problems）”。
不要一看到“问题（problems）”就去找特定的困难词汇，原文是通过罗列一堆具体的糟糕路况细节来具象化这个麻烦的。

Streets were dirty, rubbish was everywhere and the British climate did not help. Walking could be a risky business. The terrible state of roads, always flooded and muddy, created a metropolitan world of shoe cleaners and street sweepers.

questions.question: a mention of the tough qualities of men’s shoes

analyses.content: E段指出男鞋完全由皮革制成，提供了对雨水、泥泞和恶劣天气的“抵抗力（resistance）”，这就是题目所说的“坚固耐用（tough qualities）”。
你可能只看到了男鞋的样式，但一定要找到“抵抗恶劣天气”这种能具体体现“tough（坚固）”特质的功能描述才算精准定位。
Men wore more sober footwear, not unlike modern shoes. Their shoes were entirely made of leather, which provided resistance to rain, mud and bad weather.

questions.question: a reference to modes of transport used by visitors to London

analyses.content: B段提到去伦敦的观光客��sightseer，对应visitors）的旅程通常需要乘坐“船和马车（boats and coaches）”，这就直接对应了题目中的“交通方式（modes of transport）”。
你可能看到其他段落提到走路就急着选，但题目明确问的是“去伦敦的游客（visitors to London）”所使用的代步工具。
For instance, in eighteenth-century London, a sightseer’s experience was restricted to touristic places and involved journeys by a series of boats and coaches.

questions.question: a mention of the limited areas in early eighteenth-century London where local people could enjoy walking

analyses.content: A段指出在世纪上半叶，由于街道状况太差，人们只能在“私人公园或游乐园（private parks or pleasure gardens）”里面进行休闲散步，对应了题目中18世纪初期“有限的区域（limited areas）”。
你可能看到了C段提到的公共散步空间，但C段讲的是世纪中叶空间变多的情况，题目问的是18世纪初期的“有限”区域。

During the first half of that century, the physical mobility of the upper classes in the city had been considerably restricted: the poor condition of the streets did not allow ‘walking for pleasure’ outside private parks or pleasure gardens.

analyses.content: F段指出富裕女性的鞋子会通过匹配的面料、颜色、刺绣或搭扣，与她们的其他衣物“保持和谐（harmonised with）”，完美对应选项A的设计与裙子“相配（match）”。
你可能会觉得刺绣和搭扣只是单纯的鞋子装饰，但原文明确说明了这些细节设计的初衷是为了和衣服保持“匹配（matching）”。

The shoes of men and women related to their more general clothing in different ways. Wealthy women’s footwear harmonised with their other garments, a harmony that could be effected through matching textiles, general colour, embroidered detail or buckles.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are mentioned?

analyses.content: F段明确提到，上流社会男性的鞋子作为一种标志，将他们与“年轻男孩、女性”以及“工人”区分开来（distinguished），直接对应选项D的“将穿着者与其他群体区分开（set the wearer apart from other groups）”。
你可能被前面各种鲜艳颜色的描述吸引了注意力，但只有找到明确提到将男性与其他三类人“区分开（emphasised the difference / distinguished）”的地方，才能锁定答案。

The shoe of an upper-class man also acted as a type of sign which emphasised the difference between the wearer and young boys and women. The shoe also distinguished him from working men who wore leather or cloth protective leggings, ragged shoes and clogs.

groups.contentHtml:
Walking in the eighteenth century
Only a few texts dating from the first few decades of the eighteenth century actually make reference to walking. In fact, in London, only people who were less well-off had to walk rather than take a . The situation, though, was different in the .
Things changed mid-century, as more public spaces for walking were made available in London, and a number of English cities were affected by similar governmental decisions during the second half of the century. As a consequence, according to Sophie von La Roche, the number of rose dramatically, because many people were able to walk on wide away from the traffic.

analyses.content: B段指出，散步被认为是社会较穷阶层的活动，或者是那些买不起“马车（coach）”的人的活动，对应填空题中较穷的人只能走路而不是乘坐马车。
填空时要注意词性限制以及单复数，原文是“a coach”，题目空前也有“a”，因此直接填单数“coach”即可，不要自己加复数。
Walking was considered to be an activity for the poorer members of society — or simply those who could not afford a coach.
B段提到关于散步记录不多这件事，在城市比在“乡村（countryside）”更真实，因为乡村生活总是被户外活动主导，对应了题目中这两种情况有所“不同（different）”。
你可能会顺着上文继续找伦敦的具体地点，但句子开头的“This is truer for urban spaces than for...”通过对比直接点出了不同之处在于“乡村（countryside）”。

B References to walking are not abundant in early eighteenth-century texts. This is truer for urban spaces than for places in the countryside, where country life had always been dominated by a lifestyle of outdoor activities.
C段中提到了Sophie von La Roche的日记，她评论说宽阔干净的人行道上有更多的“行人（pedestrians）”，直接对应题目中的“行人数量大幅增加（rose dramatically）”。
定位到人名后，要注意寻找对应“数量增加（many more）”的表述，其后紧跟的名词（pedestrians）才是你要找的正确答案，不要填后面引号里繁杂的修饰词。

Sophie von La Roche writes about metropolitan street life in the diary of her visit to London of 1786. She comments on how many more pedestrians there were on the broad, clean pavements, alongside the houses where, she says ‘many thousands of neatly clad people, eminent men and dressy women, pursue their way safe from the carriages, horses and dirt’.
C段提到，更多的行人出现在宽阔干净的“人行道（pavements）”上，且能安全避开马车和污垢，对应了题目的“宽阔的（wide）”以及“远离交通（away from the traffic）”。
你可能想填“spaces”，但是原文中紧跟在宽泛的形容词（broad同义替换wide）后面、且能让人在上面走（on）的具体地点名词是“pavements”。

She comments on how many more pedestrians there were on the broad, clean pavements, alongside the houses where, she says ‘many thousands of neatly clad people, eminent men and dressy women, pursue their way safe from the carriages, horses and dirt’.
